nameStory: The 'horned' in this jellyfish's name comes from the distinctive horn-like projections that stick out from its bell-shaped body, giving it an almost alien appearance. Unlike typical jellyfish that drift freely through the water, this species is 'stalked' because it attaches itself to surfaces with a stem-like stalk. The scientific name 'quadricornis' means 'four-horned,' referring to its characteristic four prominent projections.
description: The Horned Stalked Jellyfish is a fascinating marine creature that looks more like an underwater flower than a traditional jellyfish. Instead of swimming freely, it anchors itself to rocks, seaweed, or other surfaces using a flexible stalk, with its bell-shaped body facing upward like an inverted umbrella. The most striking feature is its four prominent horn-like arms that extend outward from the bell. These unusual jellyfish are typically small, measuring just a few inches across their bell.

idTips.label: Four Horn-like Arms
idTips.description: Look for four distinct, finger-like projections extending from the bell margin, each tipped with clusters of short tentacles that feel sticky to the touch

idTips.label: Stalked Attachment
idTips.description: The body sits atop a flexible, rubbery stalk that firmly attaches to hard surfaces - you can gently wiggle it but it won't come loose easily

idTips.label: Bell Shape
idTips.description: The main body forms a shallow, cup-shaped bell that's firm but slightly squishy, like a thick rubber eraser

idTips.label: Upward Orientation
idTips.description: Unlike free-swimming jellyfish, the bell always faces upward like a flower, with the tentacle-tipped arms reaching toward the surface

idTips.label: Translucent Appearance
idTips.description: The entire body has a glassy, semi-transparent quality that allows you to see internal structures as shadowy outlines

habitat: These rare marine creatures attach themselves to rocky surfaces, kelp, and other firm substrates in cold New England waters, typically in subtidal zones. They prefer areas with good water circulation where small prey items drift by, often found in depths ranging from shallow tide pools to deeper offshore waters. Look for them in the same areas where you might find sea anemones and other attached marine life.

seasonality.spring: Young stalked jellyfish may begin appearing as water temperatures start to warm, though they're extremely difficult to spot without diving equipment.
seasonality.summer: Peak observation time when warmer water temperatures and increased diving activity make encounters most likely, though still exceptionally rare.
seasonality.fall: Adults may still be present but become less active as water temperatures drop, making them even harder to locate.
seasonality.winter: Least likely to be observed due to cold water temperatures and reduced human activity in marine environments.

funFact: Unlike their free-swimming jellyfish cousins, stalked jellyfish are actually more closely related to sea anemones and spend their entire adult lives rooted in one spot - they're basically jellyfish that decided to become flowers of the sea!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small sea anemones, but stalked jellyfish have the distinctive four horn-like arms instead of a ring of tentacles. Remember: 'Four horns up' for stalked jellyfish, 'tentacle crown' for anemones.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a jellyfish, stalked jellies represent an ancient group that shows what early jellyfish ancestors might have looked like before they evolved to swim freely. They're living fossils that bridge the gap between attached animals like anemones and free-swimming jellyfish.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus recorded in New England, the Horned Stalked Jellyfish is distinguished from other stalked jellies by its four prominent horn-like projections and quadrangular symmetry. Other stalked jellyfish species typically have different numbers of arms or different body proportions, but encounters with any stalked jellyfish in New England waters are extraordinarily rare.
